newsitem.title: USA: Metal Recovery and GM mull plant.
newsitem.headline: Metal Recovery and GM mull plant.

text.p: Metal Recovery Technologies said it was asked by General Motors Corp to submit a proposal for a 100,000- to 250,000-ton-per-year dezincing plant in the Midwest.

"Although the proposal for GM is not yet a contract, it is an indication that major corporations involved in the handling and processing of galvanized scrap recognize the need for an alternative to current, inefficient, costly and environmentally insensitive methods of processing," said Metal Recovery's technical director, William Morgan.
Similar deals are also being looked at, Morgan said.

"In addition to GM, we are preparing proposals for two large steel manufacturers for one million tons per annum and a 480,000-ton-per-annum facility, respectively, and are in negotiations to license our technology for the Australian continent," Morgan said.
Metal Recovery issued the information during U.S. Energy Department's Industrial Efficiency Symposium and Expo in Arlington, Va.
The company claims to be the world's first commercial zinc recycler, removing zinc from galvanized steel to produce zinc powder and black scrap.
Last month, Metal Recovery said it expected to process at least 10,000 tons of scrap at its first commercial plant which started up last September in East Chicago.
Processed scrap is already being sold to a foundry and the zinc was destined for the zinc powder market.
The technology was developed by the company in partnership with the Argonne National Laboratory and the U.S. Energy Dept.
Energy Department also gave Metal Recovery a $5.5 million contract to promote the new technology.

Since the early 1980s, galvanized sheet steel has been used extensively in making car bodies and some 25 percent ends up as virgin or prompt scrap after the body panels have been cut out. In a couple of years time, the first generation of galvanized steel bodied cars reach the end of the road, ready for recycling.
